Apt
ăpt
adj. (fitted, skilled, ready for; in the pastoral epistles, apt to teach; rendering Greek didaktikos, Hebrew phrases for fit for war)
Latin aptus, fitted, joined. The Greek didaktikos is skilled in teaching — not willing to, but able to, and able in a way that can be examined.

Biblical Definition

The bishop “must be blameless, the husband of one wife, vigilant, sober, of good behaviour, given to hospitality, apt to teach” (1Ti 3:2). “The servant of the Lord must not strive; but be gentle unto all men, apt to teach, patient” (2Ti 2:24). Of Asher's sons: “choice and mighty men of valour, chief of the princes… apt to the war” (1Ch 7:40). Nebuchadnezzar carried away “all that were strong and apt for war” (2Ki 24:16).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines apt as fit, suitable; having a tendency, liable; inclined, disposed; ready, quick; qualified.

expand to see more

APT, a. Fit; suitable; as, a story apt to the purpose.

2. Having a tendency; liable; used of things.

3. Inclined; disposed customarily; used of persons.

4. Ready; quick; used of the mental powers; as a pupil apt to learn.

5. Qualified; fit; as, all that were strong and apt for war.

Key Scripture

1Ti 3:2 — "A bishop then must be blameless, the husband of one wife, vigilant, sober, of good behaviour, given to hospitality, apt to teach;"

2Ti 2:24 — "And the servant of the Lord must not strive; but be gentle unto all men, apt to teach, patient,"

1Ch 7:40 — "All these were the children of Asher, heads of their father's house, choice and mighty men of valour, chief of the princes. And the number throughout the genealogy of them that were apt to the war and to battle was twenty and six thousand men."

2Ki 24:16 — "And all the men of might, even seven thousand, and craftsmen and smiths a thousand, all that were strong and apt for war, even them the king of Babylon brought captive to Babylon."

Modern Corruption

Elders are chosen for their success and their sociability, and the one ability Paul required is that they be apt to teach.

expand to see more

Every qualification for the bishop in 1 Timothy 3 is a character qualification except one, and the one is apt to teach. It is not a willingness or a warmth; the Greek is the skill of a teacher, a competence that can be tested by hearing him, and it is the qualification the church most often waives. Boards are filled with men of business sense, men of standing, men who are liked, and the question whether they can open a passage of Scripture and make it plain is not asked. Paul asked nothing else of the elder's gifts. Second Timothy 2:24 sets the aptness in its company — gentle unto all men, apt to teach, patient, in meekness instructing those that oppose themselves — because teaching in the church is done to people who resist it, and the apt teacher is the one who can keep teaching when they do.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek didaktikos (G1317), skilled in teaching, apt to teach; Hebrew asah milchamah (H6213, H4421), to make war; yatsa tsaba (H3318, H6635), to go out to war.

expand to see more

Greek didaktikos (G1317) — apt to teach; 1 Timothy 3:2, 2 Timothy 2:24 only.

Hebrew osei milchamah (H6213, H4421) — makers of war, apt for war; 2 Kings 24:16; yotse tsaba (H3318, H6635), 1 Chronicles 7:40.

Usage

"“Apt to teach” — the one gift the elder must have."

"“Gentle unto all men, apt to teach, patient” — teaching people who resist it."

"“Strong and apt for war” — the men Nebuchadnezzar took."
